AGENT PERMISSION CONFIG CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your AI coding agent's permission config over-broad?

Paste your Claude Code .claude/settings.json, or an .mcp.json / .cursor/mcp.json / .vscode/mcp.json MCP-server config, and see every blanket Bash allow-all rule, unscoped destructive-command allow with no matching deny rule, MCP server reached over plain http://, and hardcoded-looking secret sitting in a server's env or headers instead of an environment-variable reference.

Nothing is uploaded. The JSON you paste is parsed entirely in this browser and never sent anywhere. This tool never launches a server's command and never contacts a server's URL — it only reads the text you give it.

1. Paste your config

2. What was found

SeverityCheckDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it also flags whether a config carrying a hardcoded-looking secret is tracked by git:

node cli.mjs check                          # auto-discovers config files under .
node cli.mjs check --root               # auto-discovers under 
node cli.mjs check --file  [--file ...] # check specific file(s)
node cli.mjs check --json

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the config file(s) it finds or is told about, plus a best-effort local git ls-files check on the same file — no network call, ever. Exits 1 if any high/medium finding is present, so it works as a CI gate on the same pull request that adds or edits the config.

What's checked

CheckHow
Blanket Bash allow-allA permissions.allow entry of bare "Bash" or "Bash(*)" — every shell command runs with no prompt
Unscoped destructive commandAn unscoped allow entry for a command family whose blast radius is large (sudo, rm, curl, wget, chmod, eval, dd, mkfs, shutdown, reboot), with no matching deny rule for the same command
Plain-http MCP serverAn mcpServers entry whose url starts with http:// instead of https://
Hardcoded-looking secretAn mcpServers entry's env or headers value that is a literal matching a known API-token format (high confidence) or a long, space-free, unrecognised literal (medium confidence), instead of an ${VAR}-style reference
No deny rules at allInformational only: allow is non-empty and deny is completely empty, so nothing blocks a future edit from widening allow

This is a static shape-matcher, not a runtime guard and not a secret-verification service — it never launches a server's command, never contacts a server's url, and never checks whether a flagged value is a real, live credential. A clean result is not a certification that your config is safe; a flagged one is not proof a value is a secret. See why these configs are worth linting, and where this checker's own edges are, or this checker vs. reading the JSON by eye.

Common questions

Why does a Bash allow-all rule matter?

Claude Code's permission rules scope a tool by an optional pattern, e.g. Bash(git diff:*). A bare "Bash", or a pattern whose scope is itself a wildcard, grants every shell command with no prompt at all — functionally the same as disabling permission prompts for the one tool an agent can use to do almost anything else on the machine, including reading other credentials, modifying git history, or making arbitrary network requests via curl.

Why flag a plain http:// MCP server URL?

An MCP server reached over http:// sends every request, including any bearer token or API key in its headers, unencrypted on the wire. Anyone on the same network path can read or tamper with it. This is worth catching mechanically because a config that started as a local http://localhost dev server during setup is easy to copy into a shared or committed file without ever switching to https://.

Does this tool run, connect to, or attack anything the config describes?

No. It only reads the JSON text you give it (pasted, or a local file when using the CLI) and looks for known-risky shapes in it — it never launches an MCP server's command, never makes a network request to a server's url, and never sends a value anywhere to test whether it is a real, live credential.

How confident is the hardcoded-secret check?

A value matching a known token format (an Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, Slack, AWS, Google, GitLab, or npm token prefix) is reported at high confidence. A long, space-free, unrecognised literal is reported at medium confidence — flagged because it looks more like a token than a normal setting, not because it is proven to be a secret. Either way, verify by reading the value yourself before rotating anything.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a careful read of your own config. It reports whether your config contains one of a fixed, named set of risky shapes — nothing more, and a clean result is not a guarantee that the config is safe or that no other risk exists. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for rotating any credential you have reason to believe was exposed. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The JSON you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: Agent Instructions Drift Check checks whether your AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md still matches what the repo actually has, not what your agent is allowed to run. MCP Supply-Chain Watch monitors an already-connected remote MCP server's own tool schema for change over time — a different question from whether your local config grants it too much up front.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manual-config-review.html.text:
← back to Agent Permission Config Check

This checker vs. reading the JSON by eye

Opening settings.json or an mcpServers block and skimming it before committing is a normal way to catch an obvious problem once, and it works fine for a two-server config checked right after you write it. It is a different job from confirming the config is still tight today, after every onboarding session or MCP server someone else has added since -- most of which nobody thinks to re-read, because they didn't add it themselves.

Where reading it by eye usually goes wrong

StepCommon gap by eyeWhat this checker does
Spotting a Bash allow-all ruleObvious in a two-line example; buried and easy to skim past among dozens of narrowly-scoped rule strings in a config that grew over months of onboarding.Flags a bare "Bash" or "Bash(*)" entry by rule, every time, regardless of how many other rules surround it.
Spotting an unscoped destructive commandRequires recognizing that Bash(rm) with no colon-scoped path is functionally unlimited -- easy to read as "the same shape as the other rules" without checking each one's scope.Checks every allow rule's scope and cross-references it against the deny list in the same pass.
Spotting a plain-http MCP urlA url that looks superficially fine (a real domain, a real path) is easy to approve without noticing it starts with http:// rather than https://.Checks the literal scheme of every server's url, every time.
Spotting a hardcoded token in env/headersObvious in a two-line example; much less obvious in a real server block where most values legitimately are literals (a model name, a log level) and the one live token blends in.Applies the same known-token-format and reference-pattern check to every env/headers value, every server, every time.
Re-checking after later, unrelated changesNothing prompts a re-read of a server block you didn't just add -- drift accumulates silently between the checks that do happen.Costs nothing to re-run; wiring the CLI into CI on every PR makes the re-check automatic rather than something to remember.

Common questions

What's wrong with just reading settings.json myself before committing it?

Nothing, for a short config checked once. It stops scaling the way these files actually grow: an mcpServers block that accumulates entries from several onboarding sessions means re-reading all of them, correctly, every time anyone adds or edits one — and nobody re-checks a server block they didn't just touch. This tool checks every allow/deny rule and every server entry the same way, every time you run it, in the time it takes to paste the file in.

Isn't a hardcoded API key obvious when you're looking at the file?

It is obvious in a two-line example. It is much less obvious in a real mcpServers block with several servers, each carrying a handful of env or header entries, most of which are legitimately literal (a model name, a port number, a log level) — the one entry that is a live token blends into the rest unless something specifically checks each value's shape. This tool applies the same known-token-format and reference-pattern checks to every value, every time, rather than relying on a reviewer's eye catching the one that matters.

Wouldn't code review catch a Bash allow-all rule?

Only if the reviewer already treats permission config with the same scrutiny as application code — and settings.json / .mcp.json are usually written once during setup, outside the normal review flow that catches a risky application-code change. Even when it is reviewed, "Bash" and "Bash(*)" read as ordinary configuration next to dozens of other rule strings unless the reviewer is specifically looking for the allow-all shape. This tool flags it by rule, every time, regardless of whether the reviewer already knows to look.

Is anything I check here uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the JSON you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends any of it anywhere — exactly like the rest of this tool. The CLI reads only local files, with no network call, ever.

Try it

node cli.mjs check --root .
node cli.mjs check --file .mcp.json --json

Exits 1 if any high/medium finding is present, so it works as a CI gate on the same PR that adds a server or widens a permission rule. See why these configs need a linter, and this checker's own named limits.

No warranty. This tool reports whether your config contains one of a fixed, named set of risky shapes — nothing more, and a clean result is not a guarantee that your configuration is safe. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a careful read of your own config. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for rotating any credential you have reason to believe was exposed. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; the JSON you paste is never uploaded anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

why-ai-agent-permission-configs-need-a-l.text:
← Back to Agent Permission Config Check

Why AI coding agent permission configs need a linter

Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code's Copilot agent mode all read a project-level config that decides what an AI coding agent is allowed to do without asking first, and which external MCP servers it can reach. Claude Code's own .claude/settings.json carries a permissions block (allow, deny, ask rule lists); Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code all read an mcpServers block from a project file (.mcp.json, .cursor/mcp.json, .vscode/mcp.json respectively) in the same JSON shape. None of it is reviewed the way application code is — it is typically written once, during setup, by whoever got the agent running fastest.

Why the shape drifts wide, not narrow

The failure mode is not malice, it's friction. A permission prompt that interrupts every git status or npm test gets widened to a bare "Bash" allow rule the first time it becomes annoying, and nothing narrows it back afterward because the agent stops asking. An MCP server config copied from a blog post or a colleague's machine during a quick setup keeps its http://localhost URL and its inline API key exactly as written, because switching to an environment-variable reference is a second step nobody was blocked on taking. Both are one-line permission edits with no reviewer and no test suite — the same unforced-drift shape this repository's own agent-instructions-drift-check documents for instruction files, applied to what the agent is allowed to do rather than what it is told.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

CheckSourceOut of scope for v0
Blanket Bash allow-allA bare "Bash" or "Bash(*)" entry in permissions.allowNon-Bash tools (Read, Write, WebFetch) granted broadly — real risk, but a much noisier, product-specific judgment about what "too broad" means for a file-editing or fetch tool
Unscoped destructive commandAn unscoped allow entry for sudo, rm, curl, wget, chmod, eval, dd, mkfs, shutdown, or reboot, with no matching denyAny other command; this is a short, named list of the highest-blast-radius families, not an exhaustive taxonomy
Plain-http MCP serverAn mcpServers entry's url starting with http://Whether the server itself is trustworthy, malicious, or compromised — this tool never contacts it
Hardcoded-looking secretA literal env/headers value matching a known token format (high confidence) or a long unrecognised literal (medium confidence)Verifying the value is a real, live credential — this tool never sends it anywhere to test that

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Run it on every pull request that touches a permission or MCP config file:

- name: Check agent permission/MCP config
  run: node ventures/agent-permission-config-check/cli.mjs check --root .

The command exits non-zero if any high or medium finding is present — so the same pull request that widens an allow rule or adds an MCP server is the one that has to justify it.

Common questions

Isn't this just a secret scanner?

General secret scanners (gitleaks, trufflehog) look for token-shaped strings anywhere in a repository's history and files, which overlaps with this tool's hardcoded-secret check. They do not parse permissions.allow/deny/ask rules for an allow-all Bash grant or an unscoped destructive command, and they do not know the mcpServers JSON shape well enough to flag a plain-http url specifically — both specific to how an AI coding agent's own permission config, rather than application code, grants risk.

Why only these four checks?

Each is a deterministic, no-false-negative-by-construction shape: a rule string either matches the allow-all pattern or it doesn't, a url either starts with http:// or it doesn't. That is deliberately narrower than a full policy review — it catches the small number of shapes that are almost never intentional, not every possible over-broad grant, which would require understanding what the repo's own workflows actually need.

Does a clean result mean the config is safe?

No. A narrowly-scoped allow list can still grant more than a given workflow needs, and a config with no MCP servers at all trivially passes every MCP-related check. This tool proves the absence of four specific, named risky shapes — it does not and cannot prove the presence of safety.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether your config contains one of a fixed, named set of risky shapes — nothing more. It is not security advice, and a clean result is not a guarantee that your configuration is safe. Verify by reading the actual files before relying on it, and rotate any credential you have reason to believe was exposed. Back to the tool.
